newsitem.title: USA: Two brokers plead guilty in $75 million swindle.
newsitem.headline: Two brokers plead guilty in $75 million swindle.

text.p: Two stockbrokers, accused with 11 others of swindling clients out of more than $75 million, pleaded guilty Monday to lying to investors, manipulating markets and making unauthorised trades.
The two have agreed to cooperate with prosecutors.

Matthew Hirsch and Garvey Fox had worked for the now defunct investment firm of A. R. Baron & Co. The high-living stockbrokers used some of their clients' life savings on expensive dinners, strip-club lap dances and luxury cars, prosecutors said.
They were charged last month in a 228-page, 174-count indictment in Manhattan Supreme Court.

Both defendents pleaded to one count, enterprise corruption. If convicted, they each had faced up to 25 years in prison on the one count alone. But because they agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, the sentence is expected to be anywhere from one to three years in prison, prosecutors said.

In pleading guilty, Fox, of Stratford, Conn., told Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Edward McLaughin that while working at Baron he became aware that the "company was nothing more than a group of people who got together to commit securities fraud."
Hirsch of New York City also told the judge of his involvement in "manipulating the market" and confessed that he did not tell clients "the full extent of the fraud."
"We found the conduct of these two defendants somewhat less egregious," John Moscow, the assistant district attorney in the case, told the judge. "They came forward rather quickly."
Among the stocks the two men were accused of manipulating was Advanced Mammography Systems, Symbollon, Inc. Aqua Care Systems and Laser Video Network.
Manipulation allegedly involved refusal to follow client instructions to sell securities and ignoring or inducing clients to retract complaints and forging documents.

The remaining 11 defendants, including Andrew Bressman, former Baron president, and Roman Okin, described as the No. 2 man in the company, allegedly stole from investors money that went into a Cook Island trust in the Pacific and Swiss bank accounts and financed brokers' personal lifestyles, prosecutors said.

Victims of the alleged $75 million swindle include New York University, which lost more than $600,000; Anthony Pilkington of Manchester, England, whose family owns a huge glass-making company and who was bilked out of at least $500,000, and Hong Kong businessman Keith Hsu who lost more than $1 million, prosecutors said.

Because many of the trades were cleared through Bear Stearns investment company, some clients thought their investments were in safe hands, officials said. Prosecutors would not say whether Bear Stearns was part of the probe.
